Confidential case presentation · for independent counsel · 30 October 2026

The record before the answer.

How an integrated neurological referral became an unresolved foot diagnosis, a signed clinical synthesis, eight years of treatment and a contested institutional conclusion.

Primary evidence: 3 July handwritten interview images, canonical clinical record, GP records and subsequent correspondence. This document separates contemporaneous clinical facts, patient testimony, retrospective interpretation and legal questions.

The documentary case in one view. In June 2017 the hospital received a neurological referral covering painful feet, toe-clawing, abnormal gait and increased muscle tension. It thoroughly investigated Parkinsonism, but the surviving clinical record does not demonstrate a completed, reasoned answer to the connected foot question. The clinician had recorded a history of bodily tension and the patient's account of its progression; his final impression gave the patient's distinction between sensations greater diagnostic significance and proposed a separate peripheral explanation while acknowledging uncertainty. The patient says he protested on 10 July that the feet remained inadequately investigated. His objection is absent from the completed account. That account was signed and carried forward into subsequent care.

The documentary sequence: original words → referral information loss → neurological findings → interpreted separation → bedside objection omitted → “Not clear” / “As per above” → continuing care → institutional review.

Prima facie answer: Yes—there is a substantive documentary case requiring an answer concerning the unresolved neurological foot referral and the clinical weight placed upon the patient's words. Qualified yes—the later treatment record raises a plausible persistence and causation question. Not yet established—a proved breach under Irish clinical-negligence law or medical causation without independent expert assessment. The February–October 2026 source position does not include the underlying PAR/SIMT material or discharge version history.

The question carried through the case

The question the hospital was required to answer

The supplied record documents a substantial investigation of Parkinsonism but does not demonstrate a completed, reasoned resolution of the GP’s connected neurological referral concerning painful feet, toe-clawing, abnormal gait and increased muscle tension.

The critical point is not that the feet went unseen. The hospital recorded structural deformities, a gait with an appearance of dystonic posture, severe neurological signs, and treatment of leg tension with clonazepam. It referred the feet to Podiatry. The missing clinical link is the examination and reasoning establishing how painful clawing related to those neurological findings—or why it should be clinically separated from them.

Before discharge the patient says he objected directly to the absence of a proper foot investigation. The completed account does not record that objection. It instead placed greater interpretive weight on his earlier differentiation between foot pain and tension, entertained a possible separate peripheral neuropathy while recording that the relationship was “Not clear,” and made the preceding discussion operative through “As per above.” CLIN-001142–001149 · CLIN-001614

Epistemically unresolved; operationally settled. The doctor’s conclusion remained conditional, but the care pathway could proceed with the painful feet effectively assigned to a separate explanatory compartment. The question for counsel is whether that compartment was ever adequately established, tested and revised.

This is not proof that every painful foot symptom arose from dystonia; nor does it establish that levodopa should necessarily have been given in 2017. It identifies a specific investigation and record-integrity problem capable of being tested independently of those propositions.

Layer 2–3 · The referral and what Neurology knew

Feet first; the neurological picture widened

On 10 April 2017 the GP recorded bilateral foot pain, abnormal gait, mallet toes and pressure areas, with difficulty working while standing. By 8 June the GP considered neurology assessment of gait, feet and muscle tension; a separate occupational-health clinician reinforced the concern. By 23 June, marked bilateral leg tone and brisk arm reflexes were documented. By 29 June deteriorating dexterity prevented normal work and prompted urgent assessment. CLIN-000018–000028 · 000064–000074 · 000100–000105 · 000190–000199 · 000210–000225

29 June 2017 · Full GP referral · Dr Aaron Brennan

an unusual festinant and stiff gait CLIN-000851–000854

marked stiffness and increased tone in both upper and lower limbs CLIN-000856–000859

he claws is toes CLIN-000861–000862

The referral also reports bilateral foot problems, discomfort, impaired dexterity and declining function.

Hospital internal abbreviated referral · admission pathway

The express toe-clawing and fuller integrated account do not carry through into the short internal representation.

The existing case file identifies this abbreviated hospital record as exhibit S02. Its precise wording must be read from that exhibit, rather than reconstructed or invented here.

Documentary effect: the neurological foot question became less visible in the working summary; the later dystonic-looking examination still provided an opportunity to recover it.

The GP referral was causally open, not a simple request to confirm Parkinson’s disease. It described toe-clawing, stiffness, deteriorating movement and foot difficulty as part of one presentation. The internal hospital précis shortened that presentation and did not carry forward the express toe-clawing description in the same way. The hospital retained the longer correspondence. The content loss is documentable; whether it altered any individual’s actual clinical reasoning requires workflow evidence. GP referral CLIN-000815–000890 · hospital referral précis, S02

Neurology investigated the Parkinsonian syndrome with examination, imaging, DaTscan and specialist discussion. Its own gait examination stated: “footdrop appearance somewhat suggestive of a dystonic posture - NOT FOOT DROP.” The lower-limb examination also noted rigidity and foot deformities. CLIN-001084–001122 · CLIN-001097–001099

The discharge record says: “Clonazepam was given at night to relieve tension in the legs.” CLIN-001651–001653 This is not a diagnostic test, but it confirms that lower-limb neurological symptoms were recognised and treated during the admission. A Podiatry referral and the GP’s 6 July prioritisation of Podiatry demonstrate that pressure lesions were also addressed; neither, without further neurological reasoning, answers what caused the clawing. CLIN-000236–000245

The complex-case meeting

The meeting around 4 July focused on young-onset Parkinsonism and medication strategy, including deferring levodopa. Later correspondence says: “Myself and Tim are keen to hold back on Levodopa insofar as maybe possible unless you'd advise otherwise?” CLIN-003434–003435 Professor Timothy Counihan’s movement-disorders expertise is material, but the surviving material does not establish what precise foot history he reviewed or whether painful toe-clawing was presented as an independent clinical question. Professor Daniel Healy’s subsequent involvement concerned genetic evaluation; that is not synonymous with targeted assessment of the painful foot phenomenon.

The neurologist knew The patient's original history traced physical tension to an earlier 2014 arm-and-leg presentation and described 2017 as its maturation. Handwritten sheet 2.

The neurologist saw A lower-limb gait abnormality somewhat suggestive of a dystonic posture - NOT FOOT DROP. CLIN-001097–001099

The neurologist treated Clonazepam was given at night to relieve tension in the legs. CLIN-001651–001653

What remained unclosed The documented evidence linking or separating painful clawing, postural movement and pressure lesions.

Layer 4 · The meaning assigned to the account

From an experience of symptoms to a diagnostic partition

The handwritten pages now resolve a crucial source distinction. Page 1 records deterioration in coordination, handwriting, balance and dexterity, and a 2014 hospital presentation with tension in arms and legs. Page 2 records the patient’s express understanding that the 2017 state was the maturation of the earlier symptoms and describes tension/postures dating back to approximately 2004. Page 3 records bilateral foot lesions, prior foot treatment, less foot pain after leaving bar work in 2012, and growing awareness that foot pain and persistent leg tension were distinguishable.

That is an account of clinical continuity and changing symptom prominence. Different sensations and different time courses can indicate multiple mechanisms, but they do not themselves establish separate diagnoses. Pressure-related relief after leaving bar work is compatible with a mechanical component of pain; it does not exclude abnormal neurological posture contributing to the underlying deformity or pressure.

1 · Original handwritten interview (3 July)

“Liam feels this current state is the maturation of that.” The original also explains why reducing time on his feet made pain less prominent and tension easier to distinguish. Source image · Source image.

2 · Later typed clinical history

The discharge-history wording presents the patient's growing differentiation as a statement about symptoms being “not the same problem.” Its relation to the manuscript should be examined literally; the handwritten source must not be replaced by a discharge transcription. CLIN-000965–000976

3 · Neurologist’s final impression

The clinician says the patient had “markedly divorced” tension and foot problems “in his own mind,” then proposes complete separation or possible secondary peripheral neuropathy, potentially alcohol-related; the impression concedes “Not clear.” CLIN-001142–001149

4 · Signed discharge plan

“As per above.” The plan incorporates the preceding synthesis but does not identify an explicit task, owner or deadline for neurological resolution of painful clawing. CLIN-001614

These are not three independent accounts corroborating separation. The later history and impression are documentary representations under the treating clinician’s authorship or authorisation. The clinician could reasonably consider distinct causes, but the patient’s language did not relieve him of the obligation to support that differential with examination and clinical reasoning.

Nothing in the available record proves that the words were deliberately changed to conceal the protest. Equally, authorship and signing are meaningful acts even without a demonstrated secret motive: they determine which interpretation the GP and later clinicians inherit. The precise drafting sequence remains a provenance question, not a prerequisite for assessing whether the original referral was answered.

Text-critical safeguard: the canonical discharge-history material itself uses “not the same problem” (CLIN-000974–000976). The decisive comparison is with the three displayed images: the analysis must not claim that this exact phrase was necessarily first introduced by a typist. The further interpretative step in the final impression—“markedly divorced” “in his own mind”—is identifiable in the signed synthesis.

Layers 5–6 · Protest, omission and operational authority

Referral compression → bedside protest → “As per above”

By Monday 10 July the team had performed the movement-disorder investigation, recorded dystonic-looking gait and treated leg tension. The patient says that when discharge became imminent he asked four medical students to summon the neurologist and challenged the failure to investigate his feet adequately. This is the patient’s direct testimony about a bedside event; it is not quoted from the hospital chart.

He did not know that the original GP referral had been shortened internally, and did not know what wording would appear in the signed account. Yet his protest identified the same unresolved relationship visible when the original referral is placed beside the final impression. The clinical opportunity was to review the feet, explain the outstanding differential, seek specialist input or record clear follow-up responsibility—not necessarily to prescribe levodopa immediately.

The completed synthesis does not preserve that objection. It instead includes the patient-attributed separation and possible neuropathy and carries preceding recommendations forward. That creates a significant asymmetry: an earlier patient statement was made clinically authoritative, whereas a later challenge to the adequacy of the investigation does not appear in the completed narrative.

Discharge occurred on 11 July. The DaTscan addendum was finalised on 13 July; the summary was confirmed on 17 July at 19:30. These are different clinical and documentary events. The 17 July signature does not establish when the contested typed paragraphs were first written. CLIN-001629–001638 · CLIN-000261

The earliest source did not require the clinician to choose between neurological tension and painful feet. The discharge synthesis nevertheless allowed the relationship to remain unresolved while organising care around a possible separation.

The footprint of an unrecorded objection

Present in the completed account: The clinician's interpretation of the patient's earlier distinction between pain and leg tension, together with possible separate peripheral neuropathy. CLIN-001142–001149

Absent from the completed account: The patient's firsthand testimony that he summoned the neurologist through four medical students on Monday 10 July and objected that his feet had not been adequately investigated.

What this proves: the final document preserves the patient-attributed separation but does not preserve the later challenge. What it does not prove: the precise words spoken by the clinician, or when the typed passages were drafted. The footprint is an asymmetry between independently existing testimony and what the completed document contains, not a claim that the chart records the protest.

Epistemically unresolved; operationally settled. The clinician wrote “Not clear” about the relationship of the foot symptoms, yet the discharge recommendations said “As per above.” A provisional diagnostic possibility thus entered the continuing record without a clearly assigned investigation resolving the referred painful toe-clawing. CLIN-001142–001149 · CLIN-001614

Layer 7 · The completed care history

What followed from 2017 through 2026

2017 · Admission and discharge

Young-onset Parkinsonism investigated; marked rigidity and possible dystonic gait recorded; clonazepam given for leg tension; Podiatry pathway initiated. Foot-pain causation left uncertain. The patient's 10 July protest is absent from the completed hospital account.

2018 · Procyclidine withdrawal

Following withdrawal, the neurologist recorded rapid recurrence of an outside-left-foot phenomenon. This was a material observation in the same anatomical territory, capable of prompting review of the original partition; it was not proof of the cause of every foot lesion. CLIN-001887–001914

2018 · Genetic discussion

Possible PRKN/PARK2 disease was discussed. Clarifying young-onset Parkinsonism did not itself answer the distinct question of painful clawing or pressure-related foot pathology. CLIN-001956

2019 · Shoulder comparator

A separate shoulder presentation received targeted neurological reasoning. It offers an internal comparison for the specificity of the foot assessment, subject to differences between clinical presentations. 2019 neurology entries; issue 46

2021 · Sinemet and DBS counselling

Levodopa treatment became part of care, creating opportunities to observe foot-pain response. One note stated categorically that DBS was only for tremor, an overbroad description of available indications, though not proof the patient qualified for surgery. CLIN-002360

26 March 2023 · Severe pain and psychological danger

The GP reported burning pain causing a “death wish” and concern for the patient's wellbeing, amid pregabalin escalation. This is a discrete patient-safety escalation requiring review of the receiving service’s assessment and response. It was preceded by years of pain and functional consequence. CLIN-002635–002641

2024–March 2025 · Clinical uncertainty persists

The neurologist acknowledged relief in the feet when Parkinson's medication took effect and recognised painful dystonia as a possible phenomenon, while doubting that the particular pain description was directly Parkinsonian. Sinemet CR was proposed against the genuine countervailing risk of dyskinesias. CLIN-002777–002800

March 2025 · Relief and complaint

The patient reported dramatic symptomatic improvement after Sinemet CR and complained formally on 19 March. The neurologist subsequently defended levodopa timing, pregabalin use and other treatment decisions. The marked response is important clinical evidence, not retrospective proof that every episode of historical pain was dystonia. CLIN-003240–003271D

April–September 2025 · Institutional handling

QPS initially treated the complaint substantially as one concerning clinical judgment. The matter later proceeded under the Incident Management Framework to a Preliminary Assessment Report and SIMT review. A no-deficit conclusion was communicated, with substantial emphasis on the treatment rationale. The underlying evidence considered remains central to evaluating review independence.

January–October 2026 · Governance and missing records

The institution maintained its governance position. The patient continued to challenge record accuracy and requested creation/version history (Object A) and underlying PAR/SIMT material (Object B) under Article 15. Those requests were already made; the supplied account reports no controller response by 29 October and a DPC complaint under assessment, not an established regulatory infringement.

Human consequences

The harm was not confined to a dramatic moment in 2023. Before admission, the patient described longstanding bodily tension, coping through unusual postures, deterioration in handwriting and coordination, imbalance, pressure-related foot pain, reduced occupational capacity and growing physical disability. Over the subsequent years, persistent pain, medication changes and uncertainty formed part of his life. The 2023 emergency GP communication recorded an acute psychological danger within that prolonged experience.

Documented suffering and legally attributable harm are different questions. A specialist must identify the earliest point at which further assessment or treatment was clinically required and what outcome it would probably have changed. But the patient's continuity narrative is essential to any competent causation analysis; the chronology cannot begin with a prescription chart.

Clinical and documentary responsibility

Clinical duty, record authorship and foreseeable harm

Clinical responsibility

The referring GP presented a causally open neurological syndrome. The receiving clinical service was responsible for a clinically sufficient assessment, transparent communication of uncertainty and proportionate follow-up. The question is not whether diagnostic certainty was mandatory on discharge; it is whether significant uncertainty about painful toe-clawing was appropriately investigated, owned and communicated.

Documentary responsibility

The neurologist’s original handwritten pages, later history and final impression should be read as representations arising within a single authored clinical pathway—not independent witnesses. The author of the final impression bears responsibility for the diagnostic meaning he assigned to the patient’s words; the clinical service bears responsibility for the adequacy and clarity of the discharge plan and record processes. Proof of hidden intention is not necessary to evaluate a materially incomplete or misleading clinical account.

Missed correction points

The earliest were the referral reduction and failure, if established, to reconcile the dystonic-looking finding with painful clawing. The 10 July protest was an immediate opportunity. The April 2018 foot phenomenon, subsequent levodopa response, sustained severe pain and 2024–2025 clinical observations created further opportunities. The clinical standard and consequences of each proposed missed review require independent neurological opinion.

Legal causation and safeguards

The case should distinguish (a) breach of clinical standard, (b) documentary error or incompleteness, (c) failure to review evolving evidence, (d) harm attributable to any breach, and (e) independent safety or data-rights issues. A period of suffering cannot automatically be equated with a period of negligence. Equally, apparently reasonable downstream prescriptions cannot validate an inadequately established diagnostic framework.

Layer 8 · Institutional defence

Did the institution examine the foundation—or defend the treatment?

The first formal complaint followed reported Sinemet CR relief on 19 March 2025. The later discovery and comparison of documentary sources was a separate stage. It would be inaccurate to impute every later archival allegation to the initial complaint; it would be equally inadequate to treat an initial clinical-judgment response as dispositive of subsequent record-construction allegations.

The original neurologist’s response defended the timing of levodopa, dyskinesia risk, neuropathic pain treatment and other clinical judgments. QPS moved the matter into an incident pathway, and SIMT communicated no care deficit. The key institutional question is whether the reviewers inspected the full GP referral, internal précis, actual handwritten pages, dystonic-looking examination, 10 July account and later medication-linked foot findings—or accepted the signed synthesis as a neutral starting point.

A clinical decision may be reasonable inside a diagnostic framework without that framework having been reasonably established or maintained. Independent governance review must be capable of testing both questions.

Evidence still controlled by the institution

Object A — creation, authorship, revision, authorisation and transmission history of the July 2017 discharge synthesis. Confirmation on 17 July is not proof of drafting after the protest.

Object B — the PAR/SIMT source file, remit, author material, evidence schedule, discussions and decision process. Its disclosure may confirm or refute the theory of review circularity.

The patient already requested these under Article 15 and has notified the DPC. Non-production is an evidential and procedural matter; it is not proof that adverse versions exist or that a regulatory breach has been found. Counsel should consider preservation and applicable disclosure routes without treating these as requests not yet made.

Determination for prospective counsel

What is the prima facie case?

Prima facie here means that the available evidence, taken at face value and tested against the known contrary material, discloses a sufficiently concrete apparent case calling for a substantive answer. It is not a judicial finding that negligence occurred, not a reversal of the burden of proof, and not proof on the balance of probabilities. The duty to investigate and document an integrated clinical problem is the question to be tested; a disappointing outcome by itself is not a breach.

QuestionIndependent determination and basis
Original referral materially unanswered?YES — prima facie documentary case. The GP described toe-clawing, foot symptoms, gait abnormality and increased tone; Neurology noted dystonic-looking movement, yet the discharge impression remained “Not clear” and did not identify a concluded neurological explanation or a specific plan closing the referral. Referral and examination; CLIN-000856–000865; CLIN-001097–001099; CLIN-001142–001149.
Record-integrity concern in meaning attributed to patient?YES — qualified. The original displayed handwritten pages and the later final impression invite a direct test of the patient's account of continuity and distinguishable sensations against “markedly divorced” “in his own mind.” The intervening typed history itself contains “not the same problem,” so the exact transcription-stage change must not be presumed. Textual comparison; CLIN-000974–000999; CLIN-001146–001149.
Provisional separation acquired practical authority?YES — prima facie, not proof of exclusive causation. The clinician's expressly conditional neuropathy possibility was incorporated into a confirmed discharge account with the plan “As per above”; later records continued to contemplate neuropathic pain even as Parkinson's medication altered foot symptoms. CLIN-001142–001149; CLIN-001614; CLIN-002780–002790.
Apparent clinical breach meriting expert investigation?YES — investigation warranted; breach unproved. An ordinary-care neurology expert must judge the adequacy of the examination, differential, discharge plan and response to later medication effects by 2017–2025 standards. The dossier does not itself establish that no ordinarily careful comparable specialist would have acted thus.
Causation and consequential harm?QUALIFIED YES. Persistent pain, occupational difficulties, medication-linked observations and the March 2023 safety warning are documented. A medical expert must identify the earlier action reasonably required, whether it would probably have improved the outcome, and what harm was attributable rather than coincidental. CLIN-001914; CLIN-002635–002641; CLIN-003266–003269.
Did “no deficit” answer the founding complaint?NOT DEMONSTRATED. Available outcome correspondence focuses appreciably on treatment choices and their rationale. The underlying Preliminary Assessment Report and SIMT evidence schedule have not been available for this review; one cannot conclude they never examined the foundation. Governance analysis.
Deliberate falsification or concealment established?NO. Authorship, signed clinical interpretation, omission of the reported protest and timing of confirmation are examinable; intent and timing of individual textual edits are not established by the final timestamp.

Applying the Irish standard, not hindsight

Dunne v National Maternity Hospital [1989] IR 91 applies the conduct expected of a medical practitioner of comparable status and skill exercising ordinary care. A contested choice is not negligent merely because another clinician would have preferred an alternative; approved practice is relevant, subject to the recognised qualification where a practice has inherent defects. The Supreme Court reaffirmed the framework in Morrissey v HSE [2020] IESC 6. The standard of the ordinary competent professional generally requires evidence from professionals in the relevant field.

The documentary contradiction and the missing documented response are facts to evaluate, not matters that disappear pending expert opinion. The ultimate conclusions concerning breach, causal contribution and damages still require the relevant legal and clinical proof. The potentially stronger negligence route is an inadequately investigated or maintained framework, rather than an argument that levodopa was unconditionally required in July 2017.

Legal authorities: Perez v Coombe [2025] IEHC 396, paras 132 onward · Morrissey v HSE [2020] IESC 6 · Court of Appeal restatement of Dunne principles.

What would materially defeat or narrow the claim?

A dated examination assessing both fixed deformity and dystonic clawing; positive findings justifying neuropathy; a reasoned handover of unresolved foot investigation; evidence of appropriate follow-up reassessment; or a fully independent PAR/SIMT examination of the source records could substantially narrow the criticism. None should be assumed absent solely from an abbreviated outcome letter. Conversely, without such evidence, defence of medication timing does not answer the originating diagnostic question.

What must be proved beyond the documentary prima facie threshold?

Counsel should seek independent 2017-standard movement-disorders and neurological opinion on clinical breach; a carefully dated causal opinion on the earliest actionable opportunity and likely difference in outcome; consideration of the March 2023 safety response as a distinct allegation; and disclosure of the already-requested Object A document versions and Object B PAR/SIMT source material. Limitation, date-of-knowledge and procedural questions require separate Irish legal advice.

2018 suspected PRKN versus 2025 idiopathic Parkinson’s classification

The 2018 neurology note says “the Specific PARK 2 PRKN which we/Prof Healy suspect is the cause”. The 25 March 2025 rebuttal describes “idiopathic Parkinson’s disease”. Compare those statements with the 2017 Healy advice and the 2025 use of that opinion; determine whether the 2018 genetic suspicion was reviewed, superseded or omitted from the later explanation. A suspected hereditary cause was not a confirmed molecular diagnosis in 2018, but the shift in stated formulation deserves explanation.

Source hierarchy and what remains to be proved

Firsthand testimony: the patient’s account of the 10 July bedside protest, four medical students and the treating neurologist. The completed clinical notes do not reproduce the objection. The testimony should be preserved in its own provenance category, with appropriate witness corroboration sought where available.

Questions for independent experts and counsel: the clinical standard for investigating painful clawing and dystonic-looking gait in 2017; whether and when reassessment became required; what earlier treatment probably would have changed; whether psychological safety was adequately managed in March 2023; whether the discharge wording accurately represented the patient; and whether PAR/SIMT examined the provenance of the foundational diagnosis.

The case to answer: Where, in the actual record, is the dated clinical examination and reasoning resolving the neurologic relationship between the feet, toe-clawing, gait and increased tone that the GP referred? If no such answer exists, why did the record and institutional pathway continue as though the matter had been sufficiently allocated?

Prepared as an evidence-led case presentation, not a formal medical expert opinion, finding of breach or pleading. Chronological events are described as completed history; contested inferences, record-provenance gaps and clinical-standard questions are explicitly distinguished.
